title: I Took the Youth League Bench Rule to the Parent Group

parts.text: I watched my kid sit six Saturdays while the coach's nephew played both halves. I am thirty-eight, single dad, folding chair, thermos coffee that tastes like the lid. The league rule is equal play in rec. Coach Don smiled a lot. My kid, Mateo, still passed to the nephew, Nico, because he is decent. The field smelled like cut grass and orange slices. Don said, "Mateo needs to watch and learn" I said, "The PDF says equal minutes" Don said winning teaches. It is rec. I can still name the ugly little detail, which is how I know it happened. I noticed a scuff on the floor shaped like a comma, which fit i. Someone had left a receipt in the cup holder, faded blue ink. The air tasted like leftover rain and cleaning spray, which fit i. A cheap clock on the wall jumped a minute late, then caught up. I kept my keys in my left pocket so I would not fidget, which fit i. The plastic chair stuck to my legs when I shifted. A vending machine hummed in another room like a bored insect, which fit i. I counted three ceiling tiles with water stains before I spoke again. My socks had a hole I had been ignoring since Tuesday, which fit i.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The nephew is starting both halves again, and the equal-play PDF is in my camera roll.

parts.text: I emailed the league with times I had actually written in a notebook, because I am that parent now. They already suspected. Don called me toxic in the sideline chat. Two other parents dumped their own minute logs. Don got a co-coach. Mateo played. Nico still played, just not twice. Orange slices tasted the same. I still sit in the folding chair. The thermos lid still tastes like itself. Winning did not visit our rec field. Fairness did, briefly, like sun. League said, "Send the minute log" Don said, "Parents are ruining fun" Mateo asked if I was mad. I said I was clock-watching, which is different.
